item.title: Attack Paths
item.description:
An attack path is a sequence of steps that leads from an entry point, such as a public endpoint, to a valuable target, such as an admin role or a sensitive dataset.

Example

The following path is common in GCP.

  1. A Cloud Run service allows unauthenticated requests from the internet.
  2. The service’s container image has a remote code execution CVE.
  3. The service runs as a service account, and code in the container can request that account’s token from the metadata server.
  4. The service account has storage.objectViewer on a bucket that holds customer data.

Most teams receive these conditions as separate findings from different tools. A vulnerability scanner reports the CVE, a CSPM reports the public service, and an access review reports the IAM grant. Caizen combines them into one path from the internet to the customer data.

Concrete and abstract graphs

Caizen maintains two related graphs.

The concrete graph contains the resources in your environment and the relationships between them. This includes projects, service accounts, Cloud Run services, buckets, firewall rules, container images, and repositories.

The abstract graph assigns each resource one or more types, such as compute, identity, credentials, storage, or data, and connects those types with attack path edges. Equivalent conditions on different clouds map to the same abstract edge. A public Cloud Run service and a public EC2 instance both produce an edge from internet to compute. Path finding and scoring use only the abstract graph, so they work the same way for every cloud provider.

Each abstract edge keeps a reference to the concrete resources that support it. Every edge can be traced back to the specific configuration that creates it.

Capability requirements

Each edge type defines what an attacker must already have in order to use it, and what it provides.

Edge type Requires Provides
Network access Ability to reach the resource
Code execution A foothold on the resource
Credential access A foothold A credential
Data access A credential Access to storage
Privilege escalation A credential Administrative control

A path must meet these requirements at every step. Network access to a service does not provide that service’s credentials, so a path cannot go from network access to credential access without code execution in between.

Latent paths

A latent path is a path that is missing one edge. For example, a staging service might run the same vulnerable image as production but be blocked from the internet by a firewall rule. Caizen tracks latent paths and flags a path for agents as soon as a configuration change completes it.

Data sources

Source Data
GCP Cloud Asset Inventory Resources and IAM policies
Container Analysis Vulnerability occurrences, and build provenance that links each image to its source repository and commit
GitHub Repository settings and access controls

Collectors retrieve this data on a schedule. See Architecture for details.

item.title: Scoring
item.description:
Caizen scores attack paths. A path’s score depends on the value of the target it reaches and the confidence of each step along the way.

Value

Each target has a value. An organization admin role has a higher value than a project role, and a project role has a higher value than read access to a log bucket.

A path’s value is the highest value among the targets it reaches. Caizen does not add values together, because that would give longer paths higher scores only because they pass through more targets.

Confidence

Each edge has two confidence values.

Value Meaning
Existence The probability that the edge exists
Traversal The probability that an attacker who reaches the edge can use it

An IAM binding read from the policy API has an existence confidence close to 1. A CVE reported by a scanner can have lower existence and traversal confidence.

Path score 

score = value × product over all hops of (existence × traversal)

Each hop contributes a factor of 1 or less, so a longer path scores lower unless every hop is highly certain.

In measured examples, most of the uncertainty is in the first hop. One path scored 0.965 × 1.0 × 0.995 × 0.999. The initial access step carried almost all of the uncertainty, and the IAM and metadata server steps that followed were close to certain.

Effect on prioritization

Severity-based tools rank a critical CVE above a medium CVE regardless of context. In Caizen, a critical CVE on a service that cannot be reached produces a low-scoring path. A medium CVE on a public service with an over-privileged service account can produce a high-scoring path. Agents use these scores to decide which paths to work on first.

Unknowns

Caizen also scores missing data. An image running in production that has never been scanned appears as an unknown, ranked by the value an attacker could reach through it. Caizen does not treat it as free of vulnerabilities.

item.title: Verification
item.description:
Every fact in Caizen has a source, an observation time, and a confidence that decreases over time. Agents re-check facts in an order set by uncertainty and value.

Provenance

Caizen records one of three provenance tiers for each fact.

Tier Source Example
Config Read from a cloud API An IAM binding or a firewall rule
Agent Observed by an agent A port that responded to a probe
Static Reported by a scanner A CVE matched to an image

Caizen weights each tier differently and stores the tier with every fact, so an agent can see how each fact was learned. Static findings have the highest false positive rate.

Decay

Confidence in an edge decays toward unknown over time. An old observation that an edge existed becomes uncertain. Caizen never treats it as evidence that the edge is gone.

Each edge type has its own decay rate. Network reachability decays quickly. A CVE on a specific image digest decays slowly. When a configuration change affects a resource, confidence in the edges that depend on that resource drops immediately.

Scheduling

Caizen orders re-checks by uncertainty multiplied by the value at stake. Each agent has a budget, and the highest-priority checks run first.

Caizen can resolve most uncertainty cheaply. In one test, re-reading configuration confirmed 22 of 27 edges, and those edges held 13% of the total uncertainty. The remaining 87% was in five edges that passive probes, such as banner grabs and HTTP fingerprints, could resolve.

Agents

Each agent holds credentials for a single domain, such as network probing, source code access, or a container registry. Agents have no direct access to storage. They read the graph through the service API and write their results as evidence, which Caizen loads the same way as collector data.

Caizen treats active testing beyond passive checks as authorized penetration testing and enforces its scope and limits.

Admission checks

Caizen validates agent results before accepting them. Each result must be well formed, reference existing resources, describe an edge that is valid between the resource types involved, and come from an agent that is permitted to make that kind of claim.

When an agent finds nothing, Caizen marks the edge unverified. Caizen marks an edge as removed only when it observes a reason, such as a deleted firewall rule.

When agents disagree, Caizen keeps the more conservative value and schedules an immediate re-check.

item.title: Remediation
item.description:
Remediation agents use the graph to decide which fix to apply first and how to apply it.

Choke edges

Many attack paths share edges. A single over-privileged service account can appear in a dozen paths. Caizen ranks each edge by the confidence-weighted value of the paths that pass through it. Removing a highly ranked edge closes every path that depends on it, so agents start with the highest-ranked edges.

Choosing an action

An agent working on an edge queries the graph for the context of each resource involved, such as its environment, its owner, and the system that manages it. That context determines the action.

Context Action
Sandbox resource Apply the change directly, for example by closing a port with the AWS CLI.
Resource managed in Terraform Open a pull request against the Terraform repository.
Vulnerable container image Open a pull request that updates the base image. Build provenance identifies the repository and commit that built the image.
Change that needs human review Open a ticket for the team that owns the resource.

Agents on the receiving teams can handle those pull requests and tickets in turn.

Confirmation

After a fix ships, Caizen re-checks the affected edges. When Caizen confirms that an edge is closed, it also closes every path that depended on it. This produces an audit trail of which attack paths each change removed.
